source_text: Τί γὰρ ἔτι δεῖ; θεῶ τὰ τῆς ἀγάπης μυστήρια, καὶ τότε ἐποπτεύσεις τὸν κόλπον τοῦ πατρός, ὃν ὁ μονογενὴς θεὸς μόνος ἐξηγήσατο. ἐστι δὲ καὶ αὐτὸς ὁ θεὸς ἀγάπη καὶ δι᾿ ἀγάπην ἡμῖν ἐθεάθη. καὶ τὸ μὲν ἄρρητον αὐτοῦ πατήρ. τὸ δὲ εἰς ἡμᾶς συμπαθὲς γέγονε μήτηρ. ἀγαπήσας ὁ πατὴρ ἐθηλύνθη. καὶ τούτου μέγα σημεῖον ὃν αὐτὸς ἐγέννησεν ἐξ αὑτοῦ· καὶ ὁ τεχθεὶς ἐξ ἀγάπης καρπὸς ἀγάπη. διὰ τοῦτο καὶ αὐτὸς κατῆλθε. διὰ τοῦτο ἄνθρωπον ἐνέδυ. διὰ τοῦτο τὰ ἀνθρώπων ἑκὼν ἔπαθεν. ἵνα πρὸς τὴν ἡμετέραν ἀσθένειαν οὓς ἠγάπησε μετρηθεὶς ἡμᾶς πρὸς τὴν ἑαυτοῦ δύναμιν ἀντιμετρήσῃ. καὶ μέλλων σπένδεσθαι καὶ λύτρον ἑαυτὸν ἐπιδιδοὺς καινὴν ἡμῖν διαθήκην καταλιμπάνει· »ἀγάπην ὑμῖν δίδωμι τὴν ἐμήν.« τίς δέ ἐστιν αὕτη καὶ πόση; ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν ἑκάστου κατέθηκε τὴν ψυχὴν τὴν ἀνταξίαν τῶν ὅλων· ταύτην ἡμᾶς ὑπὲρ ἀλλήλων ἀνταπαιτεῖ. εἰ δὲ τὰς ψυχὰς ὀφείλομεν τοῖς ἀδελφοῖς. καὶ τοιαύτην τὴν συνθήκην πρὸς τὸν σωτῆρα ἀνθωμολογήμεθα. ἔτι τὰ τοῦ κόσμου. τὰ πτωχὰ καὶ ἀλλότρια καὶ παραρρέοντα. καθείρξομεν ταμιευόμενοι; ἀλλήλων ἀποκλείσομεν, ἃ μετὰ μικρὸν ἕξει τὸ πῦρ; θείως γε καὶ ἐπιπνόως ὁ Ἰωάννης »ὁ μὴ φιλῶν« φησὶ »τὸν ἀδελφὸν ἀνθρωποκτόνος ἐστί«, σπέρμα τοῦ Κάιν, θρέμμα τοῦ διαβόλου. θεοῦ σπλάγχνον οὐκ ἔχει, ἐλπίδα κρειττόνων οὐκ ἔχει. ἄσπορός ἐστιν, ἄγονός ἐστιν. οὐκ ἔστι κλῆμα τῆς ἀεὶ ζώσης ὑπερουρανίας ἀμπέλου, ἐκκόπτεται, τὸ πῦρ ἄθρουν ἀναμένει.
thought_title: The Mysteries of Love and the Debt of Souls
orientation: Clement is explaining that God himself is love, revealed through the incarnate Son, and that Christians owe one another their very souls in imitation of Christ's self-giving.
pass_a_gloss: For what more is needed? Behold the mysteries of love, and then you will gaze upon the bosom of the Father, which the only-begotten God alone has revealed. And God himself is love, and through love he was seen by us. And his ineffable aspect is Father. And his sympathetic aspect toward us became Mother. By loving, the Father was made feminine. And a great sign of this is the one whom he himself begot from himself; and the fruit born from love is love. For this reason he also came down. For this reason he put on a human being. For this reason he willingly suffered the things of human beings. In order that, having been measured toward our weakness, he might measure us back toward his own power, those whom he loved. And being about to be poured out as a libation and giving himself as a ransom, he leaves behind for us a new covenant: 'I give you my love.' And what is this and how great? For each one of us he laid down his soul, the soul worth the whole of all things; this he demands back from us on behalf of one another. But if we owe our souls to the brothers, and we have made such an agreement with the Savior, shall we still shut up the things of the world, the poor and alien and flowing-away things, storing them away? Shall we lock away from one another the things which after a little while the fire will possess? Divinely indeed and with inspiration John says, 'The one who does not love his brother is a murderer', a seed of Cain, a nursling of the devil. He does not have the compassion of God, he does not have hope of better things. He is without seed, he is without fruit. He is not a branch of the ever-living heavenly vine, he is cut off, he awaits the gathered fire.

choices.why: Clement's striking metaphor for the Father's loving, motherly aspect; literal rendering preserves the paradox

choices.english: to be poured out as a libation
choices.why: The verb is sacrificial and cultic; the literal image of a drink offering must be kept

choices.term: τὴν ψυχὴν τὴν ἀνταξίαν τῶν ὅλων
choices.english: the soul worth the whole of all things
choices.why: The genitive phrase stresses the soul's value as equal to everything; literal word order keeps the emphasis
rejected: the soul of equal value to all

choices.why: The participle describes worldly goods as transient and slipping away; literal rendering keeps the image
The noun means one reared or fed by another; 'nursling' preserves the vivid image of being brought up by the devil
ἄθρουν means collected or massed together; the fire is pictured as one concentrated blaze awaiting the unfruitful branch

pass_b_english: What more is needed? Gaze upon the mysteries of love, and then you will gaze upon the bosom of the Father, which the only-begotten God alone has revealed (John 1:18). God himself is love (1 John 4:8), and through love he was seen by us. His inexpressible aspect is Father; his compassion toward us became Mother. The Father loved, and was made feminine. And a great sign of this is the one he begot from himself; and the fruit born from love is love. For this reason he himself came down. For this reason he clothed himself in humanity. For this reason he willingly suffered the things of human beings, so that, measured against our weakness, he might measure us whom he loved against his own power. And when he was about to be poured out as a libation and to give himself as a ransom, he leaves us a new covenant: "I give you my love." What is this love, and how great is it? For each one of us he laid down his soul, the soul worth the whole of all things. This he demands back from us for one another. If we owe our souls to our brothers and sisters, and we have made such an agreement with the Savior, shall we still shut up the things of the world—poor, alien, flowing-away things—by storing them away? Shall we lock away from one another what the fire will soon possess? Divinely and with the Spirit's breath John says, "The one who does not love his brother is a murderer" (1 John 3:15), a seed of Cain, a nursling of the devil. He has no compassion of God; he has no hope of better things. He is unsown; he is barren. He is not a branch of the ever-living vine above the heavens; he is cut off, and awaits the gathered fire.

problems.why: lint glossary: banned rendering of πτωχός; use 'poor person' ('the poor')

fixed: Changed 'the poor, alien, flowing-away things' to 'poor, alien, flowing-away things' to avoid the banned rendering 'the poor' for πτωχός; the source has 'τὰ πτωχὰ καὶ ἀλλότρια καὶ παραρρέοντα' where πτωχά is an adjective modifying 'things', not a substantive 'the poor'.

problems.source_quote: καὶ μέλλων σπένδεσθαι ... καταλιμπάνει… «ἀγάπην ὑμῖν δίδωμι τὴν ἐμήν»
problems.why: The phrase is Clement’s own wording, not a quotation from John 13:34.
problems.fix: remove the John 13:34 citation or note it as Clement’s own statement
problems.ruling: «ἀγάπην ὑμῖν δίδωμι τὴν ἐμήν» is Clement's own wording, not John 13:34's ἐντολὴν καινήν wording; scripture reference misleads.

fixed: Removed the John 13:34 citation: the source words are Clement's own statement, not a quotation from John 13:34.

problems.quote: having been measured against our weakness in the ones he loved, he might measure us back against his own power
problems.source_quote: οὓς ἠγάπησε μετρηθεὶς ἡμᾶς πρὸς τὴν ἑαυτοῦ δύναμιν ἀντιμετρήσῃ
problems.why: οὓς ἠγάπησε is 'those whom he loved' (the people), not 'in the ones'; he was measured against our weakness to measure us against his power.
problems.fix: measured against our weakness, he might measure us whom he loved against his own power
problems.ruling: Greek 'οὓς ἠγάπησε' = 'the ones he loved', not 'in the ones', altering meaning.

problems.quote: he leaves us a new covenant: "I give you my love".
problems.source_quote: καινὴν ἡμῖν διαθήκην καταλιμπάνει· »ἀγάπην ὑμῖν δίδωμι τὴν ἐμήν.«
problems.why: The source quote is 'I give you my love' but the scripture reference (John 14:27) is missing; Clement is echoing 'Peace I leave you, my peace I give you.'
problems.fix: he leaves us a new covenant: "I give you my love" (John 14:27).
problems.ruling: Quote lacks biblical reference; Clement’s words mispresented as scriptural.

fixed: Corrected mistranslation: οὓς ἠγάπησε is the object of ἀντιμετρήσῃ, 'those whom he loved', not 'in the ones'; the participle μετρηθεὶς is concessive/circumstantial, so 'measured against our weakness, he might measure us whom he loved against his own power'.
Added missing scripture reference: the source quote 'ἀγάπην ὑμῖν δίδωμι τὴν ἐμήν' echoes John 14:27, so the citation is appropriate.

problems.why: The quoted line is not from John 14:27; that verse speaks of peace, not love.

fixed: Removed the incorrect John 14:27 citation; the source quote 'ἀγάπην ὑμῖν δίδωμι τὴν ἐμήν' is Clement's own words, not a biblical verse.

problems.quote: The Father loved, and was made feminine
problems.why: Odd phrasing; Clement says God's compassion became motherly, but 'made feminine' is jarring.
problems.fix: Use 'became motherly' or 'showed a mother's compassion.'

edits.old: The Father loved, and was made feminine.
edits.new: The Father loved, and became motherly.

fixed: The source says ἀγαπήσας ὁ πατὴρ ἐθηλύνθη, literally 'by loving, the Father was made feminine.' The English 'was made feminine' is a literal rendering that is jarring and misleading in modern English; Clement's point is that God's compassion toward us is motherly. 'Became motherly' captures the sense while remaining literary.

polish.changed: Clarified the flow of Clement's argument by making the subject of each clause explicit, smoothing the transition from the Father's love to the Son's incarnation and sacrifice, and rendering the rhetorical questions about storing worldly goods in natural modern English while preserving every claim and Scripture reference.
